Compare simulated respondents with real ones (experimental)

Source: R/ai-synthetic.R
compare_synthetic.Rd

Experimental. Checks whether the respondents simulated with simulate_llm_respondents() answer like real test takers. With a vector of real proportions correct, it compares the items' difficulty. With real responses, it also compares the spread of total scores and how well each item separates high and low scorers (item-total correlations). For the simulated answers alone it counts the distinct response patterns: Real respondents rarely give identical answers, while language models playing similar personas often do.

Usage

compare_synthetic(synthetic, real, tolerance = 0.1)

Arguments

synthetic

an mv_synthetic object.

real

the real data: A data frame or matrix of 0/1 responses with the items as columns (named as in synthetic), or a named numeric vector of proportions correct.

tolerance

the difference in mean proportion correct, and in the correlation of item difficulties below 1, that the notes treat as meaningful.

Value

An object of class mv_synthetic_comparison: A list with items (a tibble with item, p_real, p_synthetic and difference, plus rit_real and rit_synthetic with real responses), summary (a one-row tibble) and notes (what the comparison shows, in sentences). It has print() and autoplot() methods.

See also

simulate_llm_respondents()

Examples

# a small made-up example: synthetic answers that are too easy
syn <- structure(list(
  responses = data.frame(I1 = c(1, 1, 1, 1), I2 = c(1, 1, 1, 0), I3 = c(1, 1, 0, 0)),
  provider = "example", model = ""), class = "mv_synthetic")
compare_synthetic(syn, c(I1 = 0.7, I2 = 0.5, I3 = 0.3))
#> <mv_synthetic_comparison> 4 simulated respondents, 3 items (EXPERIMENTAL)
#>  item p_real p_synthetic difference
#>    I1    0.7        1.00       0.30
#>    I2    0.5        0.75       0.25
#>    I3    0.3        0.50       0.20
#> 
#> * The simulated respondents find the items easier than real test
#>   takers: Mean proportion correct 0.75 against 0.50.
#> * They order the items by difficulty much like real test takers
#>   (Spearman correlation 1.00); this still says nothing about any single
#>   new item.
#> * Their answers vary little: 3 distinct response patterns among 4
#>   simulated respondents. Respondents described alike answer alike.
#> * Simulated respondents are experimental: Use them to find unclear
#>   items or to plan a study, not to estimate item parameters or to
#>   replace a field test.
